title: Practice Passage 15: The Rise of Biodegradable Plastics

passage.title: The Rise of Biodegradable Plastics
passage.sub_title: Examining Polylactic Acid (PLA), Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA), industrial composting requirements, and sorting challenges.
passage.content_html:
Paragraph A

[A1] Traditional plastics have created a massive environmental crisis. [A2] Because they are made from petroleum, these materials can take hundreds of years to break down in landfills. [A3] Much of this waste ends up in oceans, harming marine life and breaking into tiny particles known as microplastics. [A4] In response, scientists are developing biodegradable plastics as a sustainable alternative.

Paragraph B

[B1] Biodegradable plastics are designed to decompose naturally through the action of living organisms like bacteria and fungi. [B2] Unlike conventional plastics, which simply shatter into smaller plastic fragments, biodegradable materials are converted into water, carbon dioxide, and organic compost. [B3] This conversion process prevents the accumulation of long-lasting synthetic chemicals in the environment. [B4] It represents a major step toward creating a circular economy.

Paragraph C

[C1] One of the most common types of biodegradable plastic is Polylactic Acid, or PLA. [C2] PLA is made from plant-based starches, typically derived from corn or sugarcane. [C3] Because it is produced from agricultural crops, PLA has a much lower carbon footprint than petroleum-based plastics. [C4] It is widely used for food packaging, disposable cups, and 3D printing filaments.

Paragraph D

[D1] Another promising category is Polyhydroxyalkanoates, commonly known as PHAs. [D2] PHAs are produced naturally by bacteria during the fermentation of sugars or lipids. [D3] The bacteria store PHA inside their cells as an energy reserve, similar to how animals store fat. [D4] PHAs are highly biodegradable and can decompose in marine environments within a few months, unlike PLA.

Paragraph E

[E1] Despite their benefits, biodegradable plastics face significant challenges. [E2] A major issue is that most of these materials require industrial composting facilities to decompose. [E3] In these facilities, high temperatures and specific humidity levels are maintained to support microbial activity. [E4] If a biodegradable cup is simply thrown into a standard landfill, it may remain intact for decades due to a lack of oxygen.

Paragraph F

[F1] Labeling and sorting also create confusion for consumers and waste management systems. [F2] Many people cannot distinguish between recyclable, biodegradable, and compostable plastics. [F3] If biodegradable plastics are mixed with traditional plastics during recycling, they can ruin the quality of the recycled material. [F4] Clearer standards and sorting technologies are required to resolve this mixing problem.

Paragraph G

[G1] Ultimately, biodegradable plastics are only one part of the solution to plastic pollution. [G2] Experts emphasize that reducing overall plastic consumption remains the most effective environmental strategy. [G3] Developing better recycling infrastructures and using reusable containers are also critical components. [G4] Biodegradable materials are valuable tools, but changing consumer behavior is essential for long-term sustainability.
